text: The poison
why: The story has already referred to the poison ("How about poison?", ¶57) and to a poison that no chemical test could find (¶248).

text: The two little dark punctures
why: ¶248 describes "the two little dark punctures" a coroner might fail to distinguish.

text: Reasoning from insufficient data
why: ¶248 states that it is dangerous to "reason from insufficient data".

text: Next day, travelling back: Holmes tells Watson of his wrong conclusion and how he came to think of a snake
why: ¶247 says Holmes told Watson the rest "as we travelled back next day."

text: The fatal night: by the light of her match, Julia catches a hurried glimpse of something she calls a band, as Holmes reads it
why: ¶248 describes the hurried glimpse "by the light of her match", and Julia's cry "The speckled band!" appears in ¶50.

text: After his Eastern training, as Holmes reads it: Dr. Roylott has the idea of a poison no chemical test could discover
why: ¶248 gives Holmes's reading of a clever, ruthless man with Eastern training who chose an undetectable poison.

text: Before the whistles, as Holmes reads it: Dr. Roylott trains the snake, probably with milk, to return when summoned
why: ¶248 says Roylott trained the snake, probably with the milk seen in the room, to return when summoned.

text: At the hour he thinks best, as Holmes reads it: Dr. Roylott puts the snake through the ventilator
why: ¶248 says he would put it through the ventilator at the hour he thought best.

text: As Holmes reads it: the snake crawls down the rope
why: ¶248 says the snake would crawl down the rope.

text: As Holmes reads it: the snake lands on the bed
why: ¶248 says the snake would land on the bed.

text: Before the morning light, as Holmes reads it: Dr. Roylott must recall the snake by the whistle
why: ¶248 says he must recall the snake before morning, and the whistle has just been introduced as the recall signal.

text: Sooner or later, as Holmes reads it: the occupant of the bed falls victim to the snake
why: ¶248 says "sooner or later she must fall a victim."

text: At Stoke Moran: Holmes reconsiders his position, once it is clear the danger could not come by window or door
why: ¶248 says Holmes reconsidered once it was clear the danger could not come by window or door.

text: At Stoke Moran: Holmes's attention is drawn to the ventilator and the bell-rope
why: ¶248 says his attention was drawn to the ventilator and the bell-rope.

text: At Stoke Moran: Holmes suspects that the rope is a bridge for something coming through the hole to the bed
why: ¶248 says he suspected the rope was a bridge for something passing through the hole to the bed.

text: At Stoke Moran: the idea of a snake occurs to Holmes
why: ¶248 says the idea of a snake "instantly occurred" to Holmes once the rope was found to be a dummy.

text: At Stoke Moran: Holmes thinks of the whistle
why: ¶248 says "Then I thought of the whistle," in the same reasoning sequence at Stoke Moran.

text: What was the whistle for? — to call the snake home before the morning light
id: q.whistle_for=to call the snake home before the morning light
why: The whistle has been heard (¶40, ¶67), and ¶248 states the snake had to be recalled by it before morning.

text: Why was the whistle heard only during the last few nights? — the snake was being sent each night as the wedding drew near, and called back each time
id: q.why_whistle_began=the snake was being sent each night as the wedding drew near, and called back each time
why: The whistle was heard only in recent nights (¶40), the wedding is near (¶67), Roylott opposed the marriage (¶90), and Holmes suggests nightly attempts (¶248).

text: Why has the low whistle been heard again now? — the snake is being sent to her now, as it was to her sister
id: q.why_whistle_again=the snake is being sent to her now, as it was to her sister
why: Helen heard the whistle last night (¶67), which Holmes links to the herald of her sister's death.

text: Why did no harm come to Helen last night after the whistle? — the snake was sent that night and did not bite her, as it might not on any night
id: q.helen_unharmed=the snake was sent that night and did not bite her, as it might not on any night
why: Helen was not harmed, and ¶248 says the snake "might or might not bite the occupant" and might escape for a week.

text: What, if anything, came through the ventilator into that room? — a venomous snake
why: ¶245 identifies the creature as a swamp adder, a venomous snake, in the room.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back? — he put it through the ventilator to crawl down the rope, and whistled it back
id: q.how_snake_worked=he put it through the ventilator to crawl down the rope, and whistled it back
why: ¶248 says he put the snake through the ventilator to crawl down the rope and whistled it back.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back? — the milk or some vibration brought it back, and not the sound of the whistle
id: q.how_snake_worked=the milk or some vibration brought it back, and not the sound of the whistle
why: Vibration is never mentioned, and the story's account has the whistle recalling the snake, so rejecting the whistle is a possibility the story gives no reason to consider.

text: Why did Julia live on after the bite when Dr. Roylott died within seconds?
why: Helen describes Julia lingering in convulsions before dying (¶50), while Holmes says Roylott died within seconds (¶245); the contrast gives reason to ask.

text: Why did Julia live on after the bite when Dr. Roylott died within seconds? — she was bitten somewhere slower to act than the head
id: q.julia_lingered=she was bitten somewhere slower to act than the head
why: The story never says where Julia was bitten, so a bite location slower to act than the head is a detail the story does not supply.

text: Why did Julia live on after the bite when Dr. Roylott died within seconds? — Holmes's ten seconds is only a manner of speaking
id: q.julia_lingered=Holmes's ten seconds is only a manner of speaking
why: Holmes's ten-second claim is stated (¶245), so questioning whether it is literal is a possibility a reader has reason to consider.

text: Were there marks of the fangs on Julia that the inquiry missed?
why: ¶248 notes the coroner might miss the two dark punctures, and ¶56 records no marks of violence, so the question is raised.

text: Were there marks of the fangs on Julia that the inquiry missed? — two small punctures were there and went unnoticed
id: q.punctures=two small punctures were there and went unnoticed
why: ¶248 says the two punctures would be hard to distinguish, so their going unnoticed is a possibility the story raises.

text: Were there marks of the fangs on Julia that the inquiry missed? — nothing was left that could be seen
id: q.punctures=nothing was left that could be seen
why: ¶56 reports no marks of violence and ¶248 says the punctures were hard to see, so nothing visible is a possibility the story raises.

text: What, if anything, came through the ventilator into that room? — came from Dr. Roylott's room, by the ventilator
why: ¶248 says the snake came through the ventilator from Roylott's room, and ¶236 describes activity in the next room.

text: How could anything have reached Julia in a room shut on every side? — through the little opening from Dr. Roylott's room
why: ¶56 says the door, shutters, walls, floor and chimney were all secure, and ¶151 and ¶248 identify the ventilator opening from Roylott's room.

text: What was the whistle for? — the snake had to be recalled before the morning light revealed it
why: ¶248 says the snake had to be recalled before morning light revealed it to the victim.
